text: Solid State Logic Ltd. (SSL) is a British company headquartered in Begbroke, Oxfordshire, England, that designs and markets audio mixing consoles, signal processors, and other audio technologies for the post-production, video production, broadcast, sound reinforcement, and music recording industries. The company employs over 160 people worldwide and maintains regional offices in Los Angeles, Milan, New York City, Paris, and Tokyo, supported by an international network of distributors. SSL is part of the Audiotonix Group. Founded by Colin Sanders in 1969, SSL began as the first manufacturer of solid-state control systems for pipe organs, with Sanders naming the company to reflect the use of transistor and FET switching. Sanders also owned Acorn Studios in Stonesfield, Oxfordshire, where he designed and built two prototype mixing consoles with computer control, featuring one-button switching between recording, tracking, and mixdown modes, designated as the SL 4000 A. In 1976, SSL combined the SL 4000's in-line mixing console design with a computer that enabled fader automation and programmable tape transport auto-location; six B Series consoles were built and sold to studios, including Abbey Road Studios in London, Le Studio in Morin-Heights, Canada, Virgin Records' Townhouse Studios in London, and Tocano Studio in Copenhagen. The SL 4000 E Series, introduced in 1979, included a new 4-band EQ developed in collaboration with George Martin, introduced the ability to save and recall mixer settings, and was the first mixer to feature a compressor/gate on every channel as well as a master bus compressor. SSL launched the SL 4000 G Series at the AES New York Convention in 1987 with a redesigned EQ and other improvements. The ability to save and recall settings, along with dedicated compressors and noise gates on every channel in the E Series and its successors, led to widespread adoption in professional studios such as The Power Station, Sarm Studios, Larrabee Sound Studios, Battery Studios, Record One, Eden Studios, and RG Jones Recording Studios, and was used by engineers including Bob Clearmountain, Steve Lillywhite, Tom Lord-Alge, Alan Moulder, and Trevor Horn. The E Series and G Series were later offered in 5000, 6000, and 8000 Series formats to meet the needs of recording, film, video, and broadcast markets. SSL introduced SuperAnalogue design in the SL 9000 J Series, which used a capacitor-free signal path to achieve high bandwidth and extremely low distortion. In 1996, Billboard reported that 83% of number one singles that year were produced using an SSL mixing console, and the company claims more platinum albums have been recorded on its consoles than on any other company's equipment combined. By 2004, over 3,000 SSL-equipped facilities existed worldwide. In the 1990s, SSL developed products for post-production and motion pictures, introducing the A Series digital mixing consoles; in the 2000s, it launched the C Series consoles for broadcast production. In 2003, SSL introduced outboard signal processors offering processing previously available only in its large-format consoles, including the XLogic family, with the Logic Channel as its first standalone channel strip. In 2005, additional processors such as the E Series channel strip and G Series Compressor were released, using SSL's classic G Series center compressor design within a SuperAnalogue topology, and the X-Rack provided a modular outboard solution. In late 2004, SSL launched the AWS 900, an integrated analogue console and DAW controller, followed by its successor, the AWS 900+, two years later, with over 300 studios using the AWS 900. SSL later introduced the AWS 916, 924, and 948 with support for SSL's delta control plug-in. In late 2006, SSL launched Duality, a large-format console combining the mixing functionality of the XL 9000K with the control surface of the AWS 900, featuring updated signal routing accessible from the center section, channel strips with E and G Series EQ selected via a single button per channel, and 'Variable Harmonic Drive' (VHD) preamps that offer standard or distorted output. In the same year, SSL introduced the Duende DSP platform to emulate SSL channel strip features for home recording, including filters, SSL E and G Series EQ, and dynamics processing, with the SSL Stereo Bus Compressor; based on the digital technology of its C-Series consoles, Duende integrates into DAWs via FireWire or PCI-e as VST or Audio Units plug-ins. On 25 April 2007, SSL released Drumstrip, a Duende plug-in with a noise gate, transient shaper, high and low frequency enhancers, and a Listening Mic Compressor. In 2006, SSL also announced expansion into broadcast video content management and delivery with the MediaWAN system. In 2002, SSL sold its organ division, now known as Solid State Organ Systems; the proprietary aptX-codec was sold in a management buyout, with APT Licensing Ltd. incorporated on 1 March 2005 in Belfast. In 2005, musician Peter Gabriel and broadcast entrepreneur David Engelke became majority shareholders. In 2017, SSL was acquired by the Audiotonix Group, with Gabriel becoming a major investor in the group. The company received The Queen's Award for Enterprise: International Trade (Export) in 1981 and The Queen's Award for Enterprise: Innovation (Technology) in 1993 and 2020. In February 2004, SSL received a Special Merit/Technical Grammy Award at the 46th Annual Grammy Awards for its contributions to the recording field. Two SSL products were inducted into the TEC Awards TECnology Hall of Fame: the SL 4000 series in 2004 and the AWS studio console in 2018.
